speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: We're interested in learning more about how you solve these cases. Could you take us along as a partner? We'd love to learn more and he said yes. He invited us to the police department, he gave us a bunch of background checks, basically handed us this book and he's like, all right, let's see what you can do. And we got to work, and basically worked out of that department every day for eighteen months. To answer your second question first, our average ACV right now is around $250k. I always tell founders kind of the same thing, go sit with your customer. Prove value, that is the thing. If you're in an apartment or things like that, get out of that apartment, go to the customer, try and find a situation where you can build alongside the customer.
zh: 我们有兴趣了解更多关于你们如何解决这些案件的信息。你能带我们作为合伙人一起参与吗？我们很希望能了解更多，他说好的。他邀请我们去警察局，他给了我们一堆背景调查，基本上把这本书交给了我们，然后他说，好吧，让我们看看你们能做什么。我们开始工作，基本上在那个部门每天都工作了十八个月。为了先回答你的第二个问题，我们目前的平均 ACV 大约在 25 万美元左右。我总是告诉创始人同样的事情，去和你的客户坐在一起。证明价值，这才是关键。如果你在公寓里或者类似的地方，离开那个公寓，去客户那里，试着找到一个你可以与客户并肩构建的局面。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Thank you, Pablo. Happy to be here.

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So you started Peregrine just over eight years ago. You just raised a $250 million round, at a $6.8 billion valuation. So clearly things are working and I would say in your case more than that, every founder, at least that I meet. Typically they want to add value, change the world, however you want to make that sound bigger. But in your case, the impact you're having is very clear. I mean, you're helping law enforcement solve crimes, you're helping fight wildfires, these are pretty meaningful things. So we're going to get into all that, what Peregrine is, what it does. But we start always, because this is ultimately about product market fit and how you found product market fit. So let's start with that. What is the moment for you when you felt like things were really working? When you felt, okay, we have product market fit or something like it, at least?
zh: 所以你就在八年前多一点创办了 Peregrine。你刚刚筹集了 2.5 亿美元的资金，估值 68 亿美元。所以显然事情进展顺利，而且我想说在你的情况下不仅仅是这样，每个创始人，至少是我遇到的。通常他们想要增加价值，改变世界，无论你想让它听起来多么宏大。但在你的情况下，你产生的影响是非常清晰的。我是说，你在帮助执法部门破案，你在帮助扑灭野火，这些都是非常有意义的事情。所以我们打算深入探讨所有这些，Peregrine 是什么，它做什么。但我们总是从这里开始，因为这归根结底是关于产品市场契合以及你是如何找到产品市场契合的。让我们从这里开始。对你来说，什么时候你觉得事情真的起作用了？当你觉得，好吧，我们有了产品市场契合或者类似的东西，至少？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, so the story of Peregrine is long and, you know, we got started by embedding in the back of a police department. We were working with detectives solving homicide cases, sexual assault cases, armed robberies, these types of things going in day in day out. We were there for about twelve to eighteen months and building product working on these cases. And the moment where I really started to feel like, okay, we're actually building a product that is adding value and being useful is there was this complex homicide that they had been working on for a few years. It was gang involved. There were lots of burner phones, rental cars, and a couple people ended up getting killed. And they had called us to basically ask for help on finding the next lead on this case. And seeing if we could help solve this. And that was when I was like, okay, we're at least providing something that they're thinking of us to solve this case. And that case actually moved forward to the point where we were expert witnesses in the trial that ended up solving that particular case.
zh: 是的，所以 Peregrine 的故事很长，你知道，我们是通过嵌入到一个警察局的后台开始的。我们与侦探一起工作解决凶杀案、性侵案、武装抢劫案，这类事情每天进进出出。我们在那里待了大约十二到十八个月，并在处理这些案件时构建产品。那个我真正开始觉得，好吧，我们实际上正在构建一个增加价值并且有用的产品的时刻是，他们已经工作了好几年的一起复杂凶杀案。那涉及帮派。有很多一次性手机、租赁车，最后有几个人被杀了。他们基本上打电话给我们寻求帮助，寻找这个案件的下一个线索。看看我们是否能帮助解决这个。那就是当我想到，好吧，我们至少提供了某种东西，让他们想到找我们来解决这个案件。那个案件实际上推进到了我们在审判中成为专家证人的地步，最终解决了那个特定的案件。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: But your product helped solve that case?
zh: 但是你的产品帮助解决了那个案件？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, that's right.
zh: 是的，没错。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: That's pretty wild. What is your product? What does your product do? Because again, the fact that you're solving cases, you're also doing wildfires, you touch a lot of different pieces. So what does your product actually do? How did you help solve that case, for example?
zh: 那太疯狂了。你的产品是什么？你的产品做什么？因为再说一次，你在解决案件，你也在做野火灾情，你接触很多不同的部分。那么你的产品实际上是做什么的？你是如何帮助解决那个案件的，比如说？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, what we saw when we came to that police department is there's been a proliferation of technology point solutions for all sorts of different types of data collection methodologies, and they weren't able to actually leverage that information to achieve their goals. And in this case with the detectives, they were trying to solve cases. So our technology basically put all this data into one current complete asset. They were able to join other data sets together. When someone commits a crime, you're able to basically request information on that particular time portion, get cellular data. Peregrine's platform puts all that data into a current complete data asset, transforms it, enriches it, and then, provides applications on top of it to enable users to explore and find insight from that information. However, I'd really say that I think of Peregrine's product as fifty percent of its technology. It's that platform that allows you to get insight, build workflows, and do that type of technological work. The other fifty percent of our product is really the way we deploy and the way we partner, and work with our customers. And I think, that symbiosis is what made Peregrine successful in the early days and something that we've tried to hold on to.
zh: 是的，当我们来到那个警察局时，我们看到针对各种不同类型的数据收集方法的技术点解决方案激增，而他们无法实际上利用这些信息来实现他们的目标。在这个涉及侦探的案例中，他们试图解决案件。所以我们的技术基本上把所有这些数据放入一个当前的、完整的资产中。他们能够将其他数据集连接在一起。当有人犯罪时，你基本上可以请求关于特定时间段的信息，获取蜂窝数据。Peregrine 的平台将所有这些数据放入一个当前的、完整的数据资产中，对其进行转换、丰富，然后在其之上提供应用程序，使用户能够探索并从该信息中发现洞察。然而，我真的很想说，我认为 Peregrine 的产品百分之五十是技术。它是那个允许你获得洞察、构建工作流并做那种技术工作的平台。我们产品的另一半实际上是我们部署的方式以及我们合作的方式，以及与我们的客户一起工作。我认为这种共生关系是 Peregrine 在早期取得成功的原因，也是我们试图坚持的东西。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Maybe to bring it all together, you go to that example where you solved that cold case. Where you helped solve it. As a result of your technology and the service layer and the partnership, and everything, what happens? What are you able to uncover? I don't know if you can talk about that specific example, but that would be ideal. But what can you specifically uncover that maybe before was just not possible to figure out?
zh: 也许把这一切汇总起来，你举那个你解决那起悬案的例子。你帮助解决了它。由于你的技术和服务层以及合作伙伴关系以及一切，发生了什么？你能够发现什么？我不知道你是否能谈论那个具体的例子，但那是最理想的。但你能具体发现哪些以前可能无法弄清楚的东西？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Oftentimes when you're trying to solve a case, you're trying to tie a person to a location at a time and place. And in this particular case, they were able to marry a bunch of different cellular records. It's hard to overstate how complex and varied this information is. Think dozens and dozens of Excel files, different time zones, messy data. Being able to connect that all together, visualize it, understand where different phone numbers, people are in relation to, like, geospatially and from a temporal perspective, and marrying that together. And understanding, okay, who is here at this point in time, who is here at that point in time, and just having that information. And understanding the movements of the people involved in the crime is critical to actually moving the case forward.
zh: 通常当你试图解决一个案件时，你试图将一个人在特定时间和地点与一个位置联系起来。在这个特定的案例中，他们能够将一堆不同的蜂窝记录结合起来。很难夸大这些信息是多么复杂和多样。想想几十个 Excel 文件，不同的时区，杂乱的数据。能够把所有这些连接起来，将其可视化，理解不同的电话号码、人员在空间和时间上的关系，并将它们结合起来。理解，好吧，在这个时间点谁在这里，在那个时间点谁在那里，只是拥有这些信息。理解参与犯罪的人员的动向对于实际推进案件至关重要。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Many times I'd say when I talk to founders of companies like this. That are very technical and hyper focused, for example, I talk to somebody in cybersecurity and they're like, yeah, I used to be in the armed forces or I used to be a hacker for IDF, like things like that. I'm looking at your profile, I'm trying to make sense of it. How do you end up here? How do you end up in this company?
zh: 很多时候当我和这类公司的创始人交谈时我会这么说。他们非常技术化和高度专注，例如，我和网络安全领域的某个人交谈，他们说，是的，我曾经在武装部队服役或者我曾经是 IDF 的黑客，像那样的事情。我正在看你的资料，我试图理解它。你是怎么到这里来的？你是怎么进入这家公司的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: So my background, I went to Stanford to take a year of science. I spent every summer working at different Silicon Valley companies and I really took away from that experience that I wanted to build technology that had meaningful impact on communities around us. I spent a lot of time working at tech companies where I didn't really believe that that was true and so after school, I went and worked at the UN Refugee Agency. Spent a bunch of time deploying technology in very hard to reach places, solving issues that are similar to the issues that I solve today. Which was the UN Refugee Agency has extremely disparate data and it's very difficult to understand how different interventions are working at different refugee populations. I joined a similar type of company that was deploying technology in hard to reach places, doing data collection in Africa and India. Partnering with governments to have interventions on one. For example, we worked with the Indian government on ensuring adherence to TB drugs and both these experiences, I took away a couple of things from it. But one, it's really difficult and challenging to work with the government. It's slow, it's bureaucratic.
zh: 所以我的背景，我去斯坦福读了一年的理科。我每个夏天都在不同的硅谷公司工作，我从那段经历中真正体会到的是，我想构建对我们周围社区有有意义影响的技术。我花了很多时间在技术公司工作，在那里我真的不相信那是真的，所以毕业后，我去联合国难民署工作了。花了很多时间在很难到达的地方部署技术，解决类似于我今天解决的问题。联合国难民署拥有极其分散的数据，很难理解不同的干预措施如何在不同的难民群体中发挥作用。我加入了一类类似的公司，在很难到达的地方部署技术，在非洲和印度进行数据收集。与政府合作进行干预。例如，我们与印度政府合作确保对结核病药物的依从性，这两次经历，我从中学到了一些东西。但首先，与政府合作是非常困难和具有挑战性的。它很慢，它是官僚主义的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: I was gonna say, it's not the obvious place that you then, launchpad for entrepreneurship.
zh: 我想说，那不是你随后作为创业跳板的显而易见的地方。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Totally, but if you're able to do it and if you're able to partner, and you're able to do it well. I think the impact there is real, and I saw that. And so, what gets me really excited about Peregrine generally is we found this way to partner with our cities, our states, our counties, our federal government to build technology. Best in class technology to the public servants, the folks who often get the worst technology, and give them really great technology to do their jobs better. And so, that is the frame of mind that I've had. We got started in law enforcement. We're building a much bigger platform and much bigger technology than that focused area.
zh: 完全同意，但如果你能够做到，如果你能够合作，并且你能够做得好。我认为那里的影响力是真实的，我看到了。所以，真正让我对 Peregrine 感到兴奋的是，我们找到了这种方法与我们的城市、我们的州、我们的县、我们的联邦政府合作来构建技术。一流的技术提供给公务员，那些通常得到最糟糕技术的人，给他们非常好的技术来更好地完成他们的工作。所以，这就是我一直以来的心态。我们在执法领域起步。我们正在构建一个比那个专注领域更大得多的平台和更大的技术。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Tell me more about the origin story. How do you go from, you know, building and selling software to governments as part of another company to deciding to start your own thing and specifically Peregrine?
zh: 多告诉我一些关于起源的故事。你是如何从作为另一家公司的一部分向政府构建和销售软件，转变为决定开始做你自己的事情，特别是 Peregrine 的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, actually a lot of it goes back to my cofounder. We did gymnastics together in college. Spent a lot of time, twenty, twenty five hours a week. Someone who I felt was a really great partner. We always wanted to start a business together. We had talked about it in college. He had gone and spent time at Volunteer. We were on what I'd call maybe dual tracks, where he was working with different types of government institutions and deploying software in very hard to reach places. And I remember in 2017, we kind of linked up with a very similar perspective on how we could partner with these kinds of important institutions to deliver better outcomes and that's really when we linked up. I moved across the country to come to San Francisco and really got started kind of in the back of my apartment in 2017.
zh: 是的，实际上很多都要追溯到

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So was that born out of what you were doing? Because the idea is very generic at that point, right? It's like, let's take data together and help law enforcement, for example. Was that kind of the first version of the idea?
zh: 所以那是诞生于你正在做的事情吗？因为那个想法在那个阶段是非常通用的，对吧？就像，让我们把数据收集起来并帮助执法部门，比如说。那是第一版的想法吗？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: It was definitely the first version. I think we came to the problem with a very open mind and from first principles. When we went to partner with the first agency we worked with, the San Pablo Police Department. We didn't have a prescriptive solution. We had an objective, which was to help these detectives solve the cases that they were working on and then we worked backward from there.
zh: 那绝对是第一个版本。我想我们是以非常开放的心态和从第一性原理出发来看待这个问题的。当我们去与我们合作的第一个机构，圣巴勃罗警察局合作时。我们没有预设的解决方案。我们有一个目标，那就是帮助这些侦探解决他们正在处理的案件，然后我们从那里反向推导。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: But you somehow knew that it was a problem. Obviously everybody wants to solve more cases, but you knew that they were probably not making the most of the data that was available to them for reasons that you saw like at the UN, et cetera?
zh: 但你以某种方式知道那是一个问题。显然每个人都想解决更多案件，但你知道他们可能没有充分利用他们可用的数据，原因正如你在联合国等地看到的那些？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: It was actually just, because when you go to solve a case, you get a bunch of data that you have to sift through and sort through. And we're like, wow, this is really hard. And it was there where we're like, okay, we need to build something to actually process this information. And then, we started tying it to some of their record management systems that they already had and connecting those dots. And those are the very initial steps when you're trying to solve a case. Obviously, there's some piece of this where we came from a background, where data integration was a very important problem and something that was front and center for us. But it was also very much a first principles, how do we solve this problem for the customer?
zh: 实际上只是因为，当你去解决一个案件时，你会得到一堆数据，你必须筛选和整理。我们就像，哇，这真的很难。就在那里我们就像，好的，我们需要构建一些东西来实际处理这些信息。然后，我们开始将其与他们已经拥有的一些记录管理系统联系起来，并连接这些点。这些是你试图解决案件时的非常最初的步骤。显然，这其中有一部分是因为我们来自这样的背景，数据集成对我们来说是一个非常重要的问题，也是我们要面对的首要问题。但这也非常符合第一性原理，我们要如何为客户解决这个问题？

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: You know, you want to have impact. So I get that that's kind of in the back of your mind. But what pulled you towards law enforcement in the first place?
zh: 你知道，你想要有影响力。所以我理解那是在你脑海深处的东西。但最初是什么把你拉向执法部门的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: I think public safety is an incredibly important problem. I spent a lot of time in countries that had no functioning public safety system and I personally believe that, doing public safety correctly and right is a very, very challenging and hard problem. And I was motivated to work on that problem, and dig deep on it.
zh: 我认为公共安全是一个极其重要的问题。我在那些没有运作正常的公共安全系统的国家花了很多时间，我个人相信，正确地做公共安全是一个非常、非常具有挑战性和困难的问题。我有动力去研究这个问题，并深入研究它。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So both you guys just kind of, you just cared about public safety. You just decided, let's talk to some people. See what's happening in that world, see what problems we could solve.
zh: 所以你们俩只是，你们只是关心公共安全。你们只是决定，让我们和一些谈谈。看看那个世界正在发生什么，看看我们可以解决什么问题。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: When we initially set out to find a partner, we were knocking on doors. We actually researched a ton of different folks in the Bay Area, different captains, different leaders who might be open to this type of partnership and our methodology here was really. We looked at essentially the org chart of these police departments. Who are the number two, number three in charge? They were maybe a little bit younger. They were leaned into technology. Isolated that list, we did a bunch of research on these folks, what kind of cases they worked in the past, and then we left very thoughtful messages. We reached out to them, and we were persistent in that.
zh: 当我们最初开始寻找合作伙伴时，我们在敲门。我们实际上在湾地区研究了大量不同的人，不同的队长，不同的可能对这种合作关系持开放态度的领导者，我们这里的方法论实际上是。我们基本上看了这些警察部门的组织结构图。谁是第二、第三号负责人？他们可能年轻一点。他们倾向于技术。我们隔离了那份名单，我们对这些人做了一堆研究，他们过去处理过什么样的案件，然后我们留下了非常深思熟虑的信息。我们联系了他们，并且我们在这方面很坚持。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Were you asking them specifically at that point?
zh: 在那个阶段你是在具体地问他们吗？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: You know, at that point it was less of a question and it was more of a, hey, can we have a conversation? I would love to learn more about how you do your work and so in our specific example, in San Pablo, there was a commander at the time. Commander Brian Bubar, who responded to our reach out, and we were essentially like, hey, we are really interested in this case that you solved. We were interested in learning more about how you solve these cases. Could you take us along as a partner? We'd love to learn more and he said yes. He invited us to the police department. He gave us a bunch of background checks and basically handed us this book. And he's like, all right, let's see what you can do. And we got to work, and basically worked out of that department every day for eighteen months.
zh: 你知道，在那个阶段这更像是一个请求，更像是一个，嘿，我们可以谈谈吗？我很想更多地了解你是如何做你的工作的，所以在我们的具体例子中，在圣巴勃罗，当时有一位指挥官。Brian Bubar 指挥官，他回应了我们的联系，我们基本上就像，嘿，我们对你解决的这个案件真的很感兴趣。我们有兴趣更多地了解你是如何解决这些案件的。你能带上我们作为合作伙伴吗？我们想了解更多，他说了好的。他邀请我们去了警察局。他给了我们一堆背景调查，基本上把这本书交给了我们。他就像，好吧，让我们看看你能做什么。我们开始工作，基本上那个部门每天都在那里工作了十八个月。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So you went to them and just kind of said, I guess I'm just not understanding if it was a pure discovery, like, hey, we just want to learn the space, you know, you're an expert, whatever. Or whether you came at it as saying, you know, we want to work on something here. This is like the idea we want to do. Can we do it with you? Which of the two messages are you going out with to all these initial commanders?
zh: 所以你去找他们只是说，我想我只是不理解这是否是纯粹的探索，就像，嘿，我们只是想了解这个领域，你知道，你是专家，不管怎样。或者你是否来说是，你知道，我们想在这里做点什么。这是我们要做的想法。我们可以和你一起做吗？这两种信息中，你是带着哪一种去接触所有这些最初的指挥官的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: We never came to them with, here's a technology that we want to build for you. It was always, we want to help you solve cases and we especially want to work with your detectives to do that. And that was, the ethos and mentality that we had. I think, especially in the early days, a lot of these government agencies have a ton of vendors who are like, hey, here's this technology. You want to use it? And it just doesn't land well.
zh: 我们从未带着这样的想法去找他们，这是我们想要为你构建的技术。这总是，我们想帮助你解决案件，我们特别是想与你的侦探一起做这件事。那是我们拥有的精神特质和心态。我认为，特别是在早期，这些政府机构有很多供应商，他们就像，嘿，这里有这项技术。你想用它吗？但这通常效果不佳。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Why would they let you in? You know, you can't just like, yo, I want to help you solve a case. Like if you have a product or you're like, hey, I just want to have a chat. I get both of those, but I don't have a product and I don't want to have a chat. I just want to help you solve cases. They're like, yeah, come, come in, here you go, solve my case. How does that happen?
zh: 为什么他们会让你进去？你知道，你不能只是就像，哟，我想帮你解决一个案件。就像如果你有一个产品或者你就像，嘿，我只是想聊聊天。我理解这两者，但我没有产品，我也不想聊天。我只是想帮你解决案件。他们就像，是的，来，进来，给你，解决我的案件。这是怎么发生的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, he definitely took a chance on us. We were very open and transparent with him in that we want to build a company. We were looking for folks to learn from and wanted to be design partners with, and he was open to that. And so, we tried a lot of people before we got a yes here. So it's definitely challenging.
zh: 是的，他绝对是在我们身上冒了险。我们对他非常开放和透明，因为我们要构建一家公司。我们在寻找可以学习的人，并希望成为设计合作伙伴，而且他对那持开放态度。所以，我们在得到这个肯定之前尝试了很多人。所以这绝对具有挑战性。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Did you do a lot of the customer discovery before this, before jumping in and starting to try to work with this person to help them solve a case? How much did you already know going into it? In terms of what the world was like?
zh: 你在此之前做了很多客户探索吗，在跳进去并开始尝试与这个人合作以帮助他们解决案件之前？你对它已经知道多少？关于这个世界是什么样的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, I mean, we did as much as we could, right? We read all these cases that he had worked personally. We learned about the law enforcement structure, police department structure, how they work, how they operate, how do warrants work, these types of things. But you really, in order to make that jump to being an expert, you have to work it and so that was our approach.
zh: 是的，我是说，我们尽力了，对吧？我们阅读了他亲自处理的所有这些案件。我们了解了执法结构，警察部门结构，他们如何工作，他们如何运作，搜查令是如何工作的，这些类型的事情。但你真的，为了实现向专家的跨越，你必须亲身去做，这就是我们的方法。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And so then what happens? So he lets you in, what do you start doing at that point?
zh: 那么接下来发生了什么？所以他让你进去了，在那个时候你开始做什么？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, he gave us a room in the department and anytime there was a case, they would essentially treat us as crime analysts and they'd be like, hey, we got a new homicide in. Here's what we know about the case. Can you help us with it? And we would be like, sure. And then, so we would sit there all day, poring over these files, trying to figure out what happened, pinpoint a phone number.
zh: 是的，他在局里给了我们一个房间，任何时候有案件，他们基本上会把我们当作犯罪分析师对待，他们会就像，嘿，我们这儿发生了一起新的凶杀案。这是我们要知道关于案件的情况。你能帮我们要吗？我们会就像，当然。然后，所以我们会在那里坐一整天，仔细翻阅这些文件，试图弄清楚发生了什么，找出一个电话号码。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Just manually? You're basically free labor for these guys, or you're building tech to do this?
zh: 只是手动地？你基本上是这些人的免费劳动力，还是你在构建技术来做这个？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Definitely free labor at the beginning. I mean, I'm a programmer, so I was writing software to do this. So that was definitely helpful, but this is a job, right? This is what they would do. They would sift through this many times, very manually.
zh: 在开始时绝对是免费劳动力。我是说，我是个程序员，所以我在编写软件来做这个。所以那肯定有帮助，但这确实是一份工作，对吧？这就是他们会做的事情。他们很多时候会手动筛选这些。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So step one really was finding somebody to let you do the job for free. Just so you could learn the intricacies, the subtleties of what the job was.
zh: 所以第一步实际上是找到某人让你免费做这项工作。只是为了让你学习这项工作的错综复杂和微妙之处。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: It reminds me of, you know, I had a company on here a while ago. A company called Ada, and the way that they built the product, which was a chatbot. Again, we're talking 2015, but it was by working as customer service agents. Literally doing the work, responding and getting hired by seven different companies. And then, just learning the job that way and starting to build tools to automate themselves out of that job. And that was ultimately it, that product. Is that similar to what you guys did?
zh: 这让我想起了，你知道，我不久前在这里有一家公司。一家叫 Ada 的公司，以及他们构建产品的方式，那是一个聊天机器人。再说一次，我们在谈论 2015 年，但那是通过作为客服代理工作来实现的。实际上做这项工作，回应并被七家不同的公司雇佣。然后，只是那样学习工作，并开始构建工具将自己从那份工作中自动化出去。那最终就是那个产品。那和你们做的类似吗？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, exactly. That's exactly the way I would frame it. It was the purest form of method acting.
zh: 是的，正是。这正是我要表达的方式。这是体验派表演的最纯粹形式。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Tell me a little bit more about, because this is the key, right? If you want to automate something or help transform, let's say, an industry or whatever. You do need somebody to let you in. You need somebody to give you all that exposure and especially talking about law enforcement. It's not trivial, I don't think, for somebody to do this. I mean, you mentioned a lot of people said no. Why did this person say yes? I mean, fundamentally, I'm just thinking about, two people with no. Let's say, law enforcement background. They don't have a product. I'm going to let them in. I'm going to give them background checks. I'm going to give them all sensitive potential information. I guess, worst case, they don't help me. Best case, they do but it's kind of, anyways, what's the driver there?
zh: 多告诉我一点，因为这是关键，对吧？如果你想自动化某事或帮助改造，比如说，一个行业或任何东西。你确实需要某人让你进去。你需要某人给你所有那些接触机会，特别是谈论执法部门时。我认为，对某人来说做这件事并不是微不足道的。我是说，你提到很多人说了不。为什么这个人说了好？我是说，从根本上说，我只是在想，两个人没有。比如说，执法背景。他们没有产品。我要让他们进来。我要给他们背景调查。我要给他们所有潜在的敏感信息。我猜，最坏的情况，他们不帮我。最好的情况，他们帮了，但这有点，不管怎样，那里的驱动力是什么？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: I think about that question a lot. I'm not sure I have a satisfying answer for you as to exactly why this person said yes. But I do think the way we crafted our message, the way we wanted to be, we had a service orientation approach, and I think that resonated with this person who was very technologically forward. And we told them, we were your scientists and we wanted to learn the space, and build, and deliver great technology for him.
zh: 我经常想那个问题。我不确定我有一个令人满意的答案来解释为什么这个人

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: They probably believed already that with tech they could do a lot more. There's just so many gaps and then just like, I don't have a budget, I don't have the time. And all of a sudden you two walk in, and they're like, yeah, okay, I could see this makes sense. Something like that, which is kind of why I have to go through so many. Because you need one that actually is already almost all the way there. Is that ring true?
zh: 他们可能已经相信，有了技术他们能做得更多。只是有太多的空白，然后就像，我没预算，我没时间。突然你们两个走了进来，他们就像，是的，好吧，我可以看到这说得通。类似那样的事情，这就是为什么我不得不经历这么多的原因。因为你需要一个实际上几乎已经到位了的。这听起来真实吗？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: A hundred percent and I also think there is like an aspect to, great, I got two free crime analysts. Who know how to write software and work with Excel really well, that's great.
zh: 百分之百同意，而且我也觉得这有一个方面，比如，棒极了，我得到了两个免费的犯罪分析师。他们非常懂怎么写软件和使用 Excel，这很棒。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Right, so you're working with these people. They're starting, they're handy cases and you're learning on the job. What happens next?
zh: 对，所以你在和这些人一起工作。他们正在开始，那是些顺手的案子，并且你在工作中学习。接下来发生了什么？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: We had that case that led to that kind of expert witness experience and we raised our first initial seed capital after that. And we got our first two or three person office. And we grew really slowly for the first, I'd say, probably three or four years. Word of mouth, our very next customer was the city next door and it was because the chief talked to that chief. And was like, hey, these guys are actually doing a lot of good work for us. And that word of mouth growth is, how we built the product and deeply empathize with the problem space. And had the opportunity to go that extra mile. I mean, we learned so much during that time. One of our first customers was Albuquerque, and I remember I was on site one time. And I was doing a case with one of the detectives, and there is this technology called ShotSpotter that detects gunshots. And I was pulling up these gunshots at time of the crime, and I was like, oh, my God, there's so many guns firing. Was there a mini war? What is happening? And the guy's like, no, no, this is. So there was a homicide, gun goes off, but there is this tradition or something that happens in Albuquerque where at the end of night, at the end of a party. Someone takes out their gun and shoots it in the air. Everyone else takes out their gun, shoots it in the air. So this homicide happened, gunshot goes off, people think it's related to a party happening next door. Everyone shoots, and so you look at the map, you're like, everyone's shooting their gun. What's going on? And so you learn these little bits of context on how they do their job, and that coupled with us constantly iterating the product to make sure that we could meet their needs.
zh: 我们有一个案子，那导致了那种专家证人的经历，之后我们筹集了我们的第一笔初始种子资金。我们有了我们的第一个两三人的办公室。最初，我想，大概三四年里我们增长得非常慢。口口相传，我们的下一个客户就是隔壁的城市，因为那个局长跟那个局长谈过。然后就像，嘿，这些人实际上在为我们做很多好工作。而那种口口相传的增长，就是我们如何构建产品并对问题空间产生深刻共情的方式。并且有机会多走那一英里。我的意思是，在那段时间我们学到了很多。我们最早的客户之一是阿尔伯克基，我记得有一次我在现场。我正和一个侦探一起处理一个案子，有一种叫 ShotSpotter 的技术可以探测枪声。我正在调出案发时的这些枪声，我就像，天哪，有这么多枪在开火。发生了一场迷你战争吗？这是在干什么？那家伙就像，不，不，这是。原来发生了一起凶杀案，枪响了，但在阿尔伯克基有一种传统或类似的事情，在晚上结束时，聚会结束时。有人拿出他们的枪向空中射击。其他所有人都拿出他们的枪，向空中射击。所以这起凶杀案发生了，枪响了，人们以为这与隔壁发生的聚会有关。每个人都开枪，所以你看地图，你会像，每个人都在开枪。怎么回事？所以你了解了这些关于他们如何工作的小背景，加上我们要不断迭代产品以确保能满足他们的需求。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: How big was the seed round that you raised back then?
zh: 那时候你们筹集的种子轮融资规模有多大？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, back then we raised, it was either $1 or $2 million.
zh: 是的，那时候我们筹集了，是 100 万或 200 万美元。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Okay, so $1 or $2 million and this was? What's the timeline? When do you guys start and then when does the seed round happen?
zh: 好的，那么是 100 万还是 200 万美元，这是什么时候的事？时间线是什么？你们什么时候开始的，然后种子轮是什么时候发生的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: The seed round was nine or ten months after we started the company.
zh: 种子轮是在我们创办公司后的九到十个月。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Yeah, it's funny, comparing it to the stuff you see today. This is, and then you end up where you end up. Which is obviously hugely successful, but it's good to remember what I would always call that reality, right? I don't know that this can stay forever, but nine months to raise a million dollars today is like, oh my god. You should be raising, you know, ten, and you should be growing crazy. But this is how you ultimately end up with the real business. It's worth billions of dollars. Most of the businesses that end up even at this stage, which is still way less than one percent. Have a starting story that looks more like this than the highlights they see on TechCrunch today.
zh: 是的，这很有趣，把它和你今天看到的东西相比。这就是你最终到达终点的方式，这显然非常成功，但记住我一直称之为现实这一点很好，对吧？我不确定这是否能永远持续下去，但今天花九个月筹集 100 万美元就像是，天哪。你应该筹集，你知道的，一千万，而且你应该疯狂增长。但这正是你最终获得真实生意的方式。它价值数十亿美元。大多数最终到达这个阶段的公司，甚至仍然不到百分之一。它们的起步故事看起来更像这个，而不是今天在 TechCrunch 上看到的亮点。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: You know, I really believe that to build big businesses. You got to stack bricks, and there are very few shortcuts in life. And I think the things that we've done that have taken a long time. Those are our moats, and those are durable. And so, you know, I don't know these businesses well. But if you can get $500 million in revenue in six months, you'll probably lose $500 million in revenue in six months. It's just, it's unclear to me what the moat is when you go super, super quickly. I think there's a lot of durability in being able to build your business methodically.
zh: 你知道，我真的相信要建立大生意。你必须砌砖，生活中很少有捷径。我认为我们做的那些花了很长时间的事情。那些是我们的护城河，那些是持久的。所以，你知道，我不太了解这些生意。但如果你能在六个月内获得 5 亿美元的收入，你可能也会在六个月内失去 5 亿美元的收入。对我来说，当你发展得超级、超级快时，护城河是什么是不清楚的。我认为有条不紊地建立你的生意有很多持久性。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: We were going to talk about a couple of tactical areas, that we can kind of go deep on. I want to talk about one of those now, because I think it's related and it's going to be kind of the story to get to PMF. You were big on for deployed engineers a long time ago. I mean, now it's like the cool thing to do. Everybody does it, right? Back then it used to be called services and it was like, you should not do that. You want product, you want high margins, all these sort of things. But I mean, you were to the point that, if I remember correctly, when you were small. Ten, fifteen people, maybe half your team might get deployed for a month on a single customer. Let's walk through that. Tell me, how you did it, why you did it and how big was the services element? How do you still, obviously you ended up scaling? So I'm trying to understand all that, but let's start at the beginning. Just what was the idea around for deployed engineers? How did you set it up?
zh: 我们要谈谈几个战术领域，我们可以深入探讨。我现在想谈谈其中之一，因为我认为它相关，它将是通往 PMF 的故事。很久以前你就很重视派驻工程师。我是说，现在这成了时髦的事。每个人都这么做，对吧？在过去这通常被称为服务，人们会说，你不应该做那个。你想要产品，你想要高利润率，诸如此类。但我是说，你甚至到了这样的程度，如果我没记错的话，当你们还很小时。十到十五个人，可能有一半的团队会被派到单个客户那里一个月。让我们过一遍这个。告诉我，你是怎么做的，为什么这么做，服务元素有多大？你显然最终实现了规模化。所以我试图理解这一切，但让我们从头开始。关于派驻工程师的想法到底是什么？你是如何设置的？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: I think the overarching principle for us in the early days and still today really is over investing for success. And Peregrine started with, deep roots in product development and implementation, and that's what we really wanted to be good at. And we weren't so good at marketing, and we weren't so good at these other functions. But those are two things where we're going to put all our points into this. And we really believe, in those early days that over investing in ensuring the customer is successful would pay massive dividends. And I think that was also, especially the case in government where it's such a high trust network. I mentioned that we got our second customer because the chief just told the other chief that these guys were good and trustworthy. That dynamic is very, very real and so, you know, we weren't really thinking too deeply about how do we build an infinitely scalable business. We were thinking about how do we make our customer really successful and so even in those early days, I remember one of our first engineering hires. We sent him to our second customer in Pittsburgh where he basically worked out of that office for about three weeks integrating their data. They had this like luau and he cooked a key lime pie, and he just completely got embedded with that department. Understood their lingo and was able to deliver a much better integration product for them. Because he understood the difference between different values in their database and could actually map all the disparate data, to how they actually talk and spoke within their department.
zh: 我认为我们在早期的总体原则，直到今天真的，就是为成功过度投资。Peregrine 开始于，深深扎根于产品开发和实施，这是我们真正想擅长的。我们不太擅长营销，也不太擅长这些其他功能。但这两件事我们要把所有的点都投进去。我们真的相信，在早期，过度投资确保客户成功会带来巨大的回报。我认为这尤其如此，特别是在政府领域，它是一个如此高信任度的网络。我提到我们获得了第二个客户，因为负责人只是告诉另一个负责人这些人很好且值得信赖。这种动态是非常、非常真实的，所以，你知道，我们并没有真正深入思考如何建立无限可扩展的业务。我们在思考如何让我们真正的客户成功，所以即使在那些早期，我记得我们的第一批工程雇佣之一。我们派他去了我们在匹兹堡的第二个客户，他基本上在那个办公室工作了大约三周，整合他们的数据。他们有那种夏威夷烧烤，他烤了一个青柠派，他完全嵌入了那个部门。了解了他们的行话，并能够为他们提供更好的整合产品。因为他理解他们数据库中不同值之间的区别，并且实际上可以将所有不同的数据，映射到他们实际在部门内谈话和说话的方式。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: We have tens of thousands of people who have followed the show. Are you one of those people? You want to be a part of the group. You want to be a part of those tens of thousands of followers. So hit the follow button. The concern, right? Always with this stuff and again, now, maybe it's less of a concern just because everybody's doing it, but it hasn't fundamentally changed the equation. Which is how much can you really do for one customer before? You mentioned you didn't really care about scalability, but that's still on a lot of investors and I think a lot of founders minds, right? hey don't want to get stuck being this consultancy like thing. Obviously, in your case, you were able to scale it. Maybe just tell me more about, is there a middle ground? Is there a balance? Is it just a matter of, at first it takes a long time but later on you have a playbook and it's faster, or is it still really custom? How do you manage that trade off between wanting to give your customer the best possible experience, which means hand holding, means going in, embedding, et cetera. But also wanting to be able to add a lot of customers, add a lot of ARR fast, which means, you know, holding those resources back to work on kind of core product.
zh: 我们有数万人关注了这个节目。你是那些人中的一员吗？你想成为群体的一部分。你想成为这数万关注者的一部分。所以点击关注按钮。担心的是，对吧？总是对这些事情，再说一次，现在，也许担心少了一点，因为每个人都在做，但这并没有从根本上改变等式。在你开始担心可扩展性之前，你真的能为一个客户做多少？你提到你不太关心可扩展性，但这仍然在很多投资者，我认为很多创始人的脑海里，对吧？他们不想被困在这个像咨询公司一样的东西里。显然，在你的情况下，你能够规模化。也许只是多告诉我一点，有没有中间地带？有没有平衡？这只是起初需要很长时间，但后来你有了一个剧本，速度更快，还是它仍然是真正定制的？你如何管理这种权衡，一方面想给客户最好的体验，这意味着手把手教，意味着进入，嵌入等等。但也想能够增加大量客户，快速增加大量 ARR，这意味着，你知道的，要保留这些资源以从事核心产品工作。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: So I actually remember this moment where I told Nick, my co founder, all our engineers are integrating data right now. We can't build any product, we need some other strategy and, you know, I think in those moments, scarcity breeds innovation. And we started building this other platform that allowed people who weren't engineers to integrate data. And that was our first shift to, oh, OK, if engineers don't need to integrate data, that saves a ton of time. And so, we started building out this other function within Peregrine. Deployment strategy is what we called it and they were, think of, maybe studied computer science. Went to McKinsey for a couple years, wanted to work in technology and then they could integrate a bunch of data. Work with the customer. Partner with them to do that last mile configuration and I think we've always thought about that investment as a growth driver, not as something that needs to be optimized away. And of course, as you grow fast, you need to invent and you need to innovate in order to save time, and free up resources. That's something we're continuing to do and we always do. But I think our frame of mind on it is just maybe a little bit different.
zh: 所以我确实记得那一刻，我告诉我的联合创始人 Nick，我们所有的工程师都在整合数据。我们无法构建任何产品，我们需要一些其他策略，而且，你知道，我认为在那些时刻，匮乏孕育创新。我们开始构建另一个平台，让不是工程师的人也能整合数据。那是我们向转变的第一步，哦，好的，如果工程师不需要整合数据，那就节省了大量时间。所以，我们开始在 Peregrine 建立这个其他功能。我们称之为部署策略，他们，也许想一下，学过计算机科学。去了麦肯锡几年，想在科技界工作，然后他们可以整合一堆数据。与客户合作。与他们合作进行最后一英里的配置，我认为我们一直认为这种投资是增长驱动力，而不是需要被优化掉的东西。当然，随着你快速增长，你需要发明，你需要创新以节省时间，并释放资源。这是我们继续做的事情，也是我们一直在做的事情。但我认为我们的心态可能只是有点不同。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Well, because the impact is on speed and margins, right? That's usually where you would see it. Was that a problem, let's say, at least on the fundraising side back then? Again, today, I don't know that it is but back then. Was that a thing that people were like, oh, your margins aren't eighty five, they're sixty percent and whatever? Or maybe the other question is, what was the size of the ACVs? And maybe that justified it as well.
zh: 嗯，因为影响是在速度和利润率上，对吧？这通常是你能看到它的地方。这是个问题吗，至少在当时的融资方面？再说一次，今天，我不知道是不是这样，但在当时。那是人们的事情吗，比如，哦，你的利润率不是 85，它们是 60% 之类的？或者也许另一个问题是，ACV 的大小是多少？也许这也证明了它是合理的。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: To answer your second question first, our average ACV right now is around $250k.
zh: 先回答你的第二个问题，我们现在平均 ACV 大约是 25 万美元。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Which means, to be clear, back then it was probably smaller, right? It was probably $50k, $100k?
zh: 这意味着，说清楚一点，那时可能更小，对吧？可能是 5 万美元，10 万美元？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, yeah, definitely back then it was a little bit smaller.
zh: 是的，是的，那时肯定稍微小一点。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: So they're not, like we're not talking, you know, multi-million dollar deployments for the most part. Where it's like, yeah, obviously you're going to throw ten people at it. You're really playing this, you know, somebody's giving you $100k and you're putting three engineers on it for a couple of months. Like it's tight, is that true?
zh: 所以它们不是，像我们不是在谈论，你知道的，数百万美元的部署，大多数情况下。那是像，是的，显然你要投入十个人去做。你真的是在玩这个，你知道的，有人给你 10 万美元，你把三个工程师放在那上面几个月。像这很紧张，那是真的吗？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: I think that's true in the short term. In the long term, I'd say you probably have better, you have better margin. Because you have invested in that customer to the point where the technology is successful and if that technology is like deeply embedded in the way that organization works.
zh: 我认为这在短期内是真的。从长远来看，我会说你可能有更好的，你有更好的利润率。因为你已经投资了那个客户，直到技术成功，如果该技术像深度嵌入在该组织的工作方式中那样。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Right, retention must be amazing, I would assume.
zh: 对，留存率一定很惊人，我想。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, retention is very good at Peregrine.
zh: 是的，Peregrine 的留存率非常好。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: That's probably two sided, one is the types of customers which probably don't, you know, they don't buy and churn technology as fast. But also just if you go through months of integration, that's some cost and the value. Frankly, that you're delivering as a result of that. So both sides of that coin probably put you in a place where you're like, I'm not doing this again in a year, you know.
zh: 这可能是双向的，一个是客户的类型，他们可能不会，你知道的，他们不会那么快地购买和更换技术。但也只是因为如果你经历了几个月的整合，那是一些成本和价值。坦白说，你因此交付的价值。所以这枚硬币的两面可能都让你处于一个位置，你会想，我一年内不会再做这个了，你知道的。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Exactly and I think it all goes back to this North Star. If a customer is receiving value that is way more than what they are paying for, then you are in good long term shape with that customer and that's the thing that we focus on.
zh: 正确，我认为这都回到了北极星指标。如果客户收到的价值远远超过他们支付的价值，那么你就与该客户处于良好的长期状态，这就是我们关注的事情。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: One of the challenges I would say with selling into municipalities, law enforcement, these non. You've got B2B, which is the obvious, the classic, and then you got B2C. And then you got business to something else, government, whatever. These non, it's not consumer where it's, you know, the sort of things they care about, just entertainment and whatever.
zh: 我要说的一个挑战是向市政当局、执法部门销售，这些非。你有 B2B，这是显而易见的，经典的，然后你有 B2C。然后你有了企业对其他东西，政府，不管是什么。这些非，它不是消费者所在的，你知道的，他们只关心娱乐和诸如此类的事情。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yep.
zh: 是的。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And then you got businesses, care about making money, ROI, right? And then you got these in the middle where it's, depending on the situation, depending on the politics, depending on whatever. They have different priorities and a lot of times. At least from a startup perspective, it's always a bit of a hard mode situation. Because you're like, it's hard to scale, it's slow, et cetera, et cetera. What do you think has worked in your case? You're deep into it. This is the perspective of somebody that's outside, the thing that gets said, right? You're actually in there. What are some of the pros and cons of selling into these types of buyers? And what helps you crack it in the way that you have, and be able to actually build a scalable business?
zh: 然后企业，关心赚钱，ROI，对吧？然后你有这些处于中间的，取决于情况，取决于政治，取决于任何东西。他们有不同的优先级，很多时候。至少从初创公司的角度来看，这总有点像困难模式的情况。因为你就像，很难规模化，很慢，等等，等等。你认为在你的案例中什么有效？你深陷其中。这是一个局外人的视角，被说到的事情，对吧？你实际上在里面。向这些类型的买家销售有哪些优缺点？是什么帮助你以你的方式破解它，并能够真正建立一个可扩展的业务？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, and I think some of this is very much hard lessons learned over time. The go to market motion for Peregrine was a very hard one. I'd say it was one of the hardest challenges that we had to overcome in the business. We had this phase of the company where I'd say we were in the wilderness trying to find that Product Market Fit. We had that product market fit, we were trying to expand more and then getting that scale. That go to market scale, was really, really hard and that took a lot of learning, and understanding on how government processes work. It took a lot of learning and understanding on building the pipeline. I think there are little tricks in every single state and county that you have to learn. It's hard to enumerate every single one.
zh: 是的，我认为其中一些绝对是随着时间的推移吸取的惨痛教训。Peregrine 的市场推广动作是一个非常难的。我会说这是我们必须在业务中克服的最难的挑战之一。我们有过公司的一个阶段，我会说我们在荒野中试图寻找那个产品市场契合点。我们要到了那个产品市场契合点，我们试图扩展更多，然后获得规模化。那种市场推广规模，真的、真的很难，这花了很多学习，和理解政府流程如何运作。这花了很多学习和理解如何建立管道。我认为你在每个州和县都有一些小技巧必须学习。很难枚举每一个。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: What did you learn? Ultimately, what was the go to market that started to actually work for you guys?
zh: 你学到了什么？最终，什么开始真正为你们工作的市场推广策略是什么？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, the go to market that actually started to work for us was one, simplifying down the message we were, what we were trying to sell. I think Peregrine is a complex piece of technology. It could be hard for maybe a person not familiar with technology to explain that value prop. So it was really important for us to make the value prop of Peregrine very clear and have our champions kind of go to bat for us. And the way we got scale is by hiring account executives, you know, across the country and teaching them. And it was card carrying, knocking on doors and doing this at scale and building the pipeline, going through the nine to twelve months sales cycle and doing that enough times over and over and over again. And these things get easier as you do more of it, because as we've generated penetration within certain areas. The next customer is that much easier. That state is more familiar with you, that city is more familiar with you, and so they have a snowball effect, but.
zh: 是的，真正开始为我们工作的市场推广策略是，第一，简化我们要传达的信息，我们试图销售什么。我认为 Peregrine 是一个复杂的技术。也许对于一个不熟悉技术的人来说很难解释那个价值主张。所以对我们来说，非常清楚地表达 Peregrine 的价值主张，并让我们的支持者为我们挺身而出是非常重要的。我们要获得规模的方法是在全国各地招聘客户主管，你知道的，并教导他们。那是持卡敲门，按规模做这件事，并建立管道，经历九到十二个月的销售周期，并一次又一次地做足够多次。当你做更多这些事情时，这些事情变得更容易，因为随着我们在某些地区产生了渗透。下一个客户就容易得多。那个州更熟悉你，那个城市更熟悉你，所以它们有滚雪球效应，但是。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: How fast did things ramp? How fast did you get to a million and then $10 million, for example, in ARR?
zh: 事情发展得有多快？你多久到了 100 万然后 1000 万，例如，在 ARR 方面？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yeah, we went basically one, three, ten.
zh: 是的，我们基本上是一、三、十。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Yeah, I mean that's the kind of classic, used to be the classic, right? Triple, triple, triple, double, double. Now it's one to a hundred in a year.
zh: 是的，我是说那是经典的，过去是经典的，对吧？三倍，三倍，三倍，两倍，两倍。现在是一年从 1 到 100。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: It took a lot. It took a lot and there was not an easy button question.
zh: 花了很多。花了很多，没有简单按钮这个问题。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: Well that was going to be my question, right? It's like, did it ever, easy is the wrong word because nothing's ever easy. You know, even the startups that are high flying, like revenues, it's not easy. I'm sure if you go and talk to somebody at Anthropic, it's not easy. Even though all the revenue is coming in. So easy is the wrong word, but when did it go from a push to a pull? Where did it go from where, at least the growth, the top line, was not the number one, most principal worry? It was other things. And was there ever, like, did that ever kind of start a shift or was it always, okay, how are we going to make it this quarter? How are we going to make it this quarter? Was that just the real life?
zh: 那就是我想问的问题，对吧？就像，它是否曾经，简单是错误的词，因为没有什么是容易的。你知道，即使是那些高飞的初创公司，像收入，也不容易。我确信如果你去和 Anthropic 的人交谈，那也不容易。尽管所有收入都进来了。所以简单是错误的词，但它什么时候从推变成了拉？什么时候从至少增长，顶层线，不再是第一位的，最首要的担忧？那是其他事情。有没有过，像，有没有那种开始转变，或者它总是，好的，我们要怎么搞定这个季度？我们要怎么搞定这个季度？那是现实生活吗？

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Look, I think the reality is Peregrine's goals are always very ambitious, and so it's always top of mind. How do we expand? How do we build? And how do we grow? And what we did last year, by definition, we have to do something new and different. And we have to either build the fleet out more, we have to train the regional sales manager, train the account executives underneath it. Now, I will say we're at a point where we have an engine in the state and local space. It can always be better. We always want to grow faster. We're now expanding to different types of verticals. That takes a whole different type of learning. Our whole idea of Peregrine is deeply understand a vertical, so that you can be successful in it and then when we are expanding to emergency operations or expanding to health and human services. We also have to go and do the hard work of learning that vertical, and learning the way we go to market because it's different. It's very difficult to just kind of copy and paste. Of course, you can take some of those learnings, but you got to do the learning.
zh: 看，我认为现实是 Peregrine 的目标总是很雄心勃勃，所以它总是首要考虑的。我们要如何扩展？我们要如何构建？我们要如何增长？我们去年的工作，根据定义，我们必须做一些新的和不同的事情。我们必须建立更多的舰队，我们必须培训区域销售经理，培训底下的客户主管。现在，我会说我们在州和地方领域有一个引擎。它总是可以更好。我们总是想增长得更快。我们正在扩展到不同类型的垂直领域。这需要一种完全不同类型的学习。我们对 Peregrine 的整体想法是深入了解一个垂直领域，以便你可以在其中成功，然后当我们扩展到紧急行动或扩展到健康和人类服务时。我们还必须去做那个艰苦的工作去学习那个垂直领域，以及我们要如何进入市场，因为它是不同的。很难只是复制和粘贴。当然，你可以吸取其中一些教训，但你必须去学习。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: But it's always been, the challenge has always been, like you've never been in a position, just to be clear. Where it's like, wow, we have so much pipeline, whether it's outbound or inbound generated. We have so many contracts closing. How are we even going to deliver on this, right? Which is typically the classic quote unquote product market fit that you read about or whatever. That market trees would talk about. Like was that ever the situation, or was it always okay how, okay we're going to triple again therefore, da, da, da and you do. Like most startups that I see, at least, like they live in that. Frankly, whether they say they have problems or not, they live in that world where it's like, OK, shit, how are we going to make this quarter? How are we going to make next quarter? And like, well, if we do this and we do that, maybe we'll make. We're off by twenty percent and then the one in ten are the ones where it's like, yeah, I'm not worried about making the score. I'm worried about maybe retention. I'm worried maybe about like hiring. I'm worried about, raising money cause whatever. I'm worried about all the other things, but not growth. So I'm curious, obviously at the beginning, it's never like that but did that ever happen?
zh: 但一直是，挑战一直是，就像你从来没有处于一个位置，只是为了清楚起见。就像是，哇，我们有这么多管道，无论是外向的还是内向生成的。我们有这么多合同在结束。我们要怎么交付这个，对吧？这通常是你在书中读到的经典的所谓产品市场契合度，或市场树会谈论的。那种情况发生过吗，或者它总是好的，我们要如何，好的我们要再次增长三倍，因此，哒哒哒，然后你做了。像我看到的大多数初创公司，至少，它们生活在那种状态中。坦白说，无论它们说它们有没有问题，它们生活在那个世界里，就像，好的，该死，我们要怎么搞定这个季度？我们要怎么搞定下个季度？像，嗯，

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: Yes, I specifically remember the next bottleneck for Peregrine was that deployment motion that you talked about, like, how did you scale that? When we started getting, you know, not like single digit customers, but dozens and dozens? And then it was like, oh man, how does this even work at scale? And I think that was a big moment for us. I would say the year of 2023, is.
zh: 是的，我特别记得 Peregrine 的下一个瓶颈是你谈到的那个部署动作，你是怎么扩展那个的？当我们开始获得，你知道，不是个位数的客户，而是几十个几十个的时候？然后就像，天啊，这在规模下甚至是如何运作的？我认为这对我们来说是一个重要时刻。我想说是 2023 年，是。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: You're now in the tens of millions, right? At that point, could you point to something? There's probably no good answer to this question. I'll ask it anyways. What took you from more of a push, hey, we're doing numbers, we're doing great, one, three, ten. That's awesome, to like, wow, we're growing so fast. I've got these other problems? And I'm asking it, you know, just for my client. That to me is that, you know, we talked earlier about the product market fit moment. Which is really like a value delivery moment, right? The first time it was an action, you solve the cold case, like, okay, this thing works. That's not necessarily the same as there is so much demand for this. I'm drowning in demand, which is kind of what you're talking about in the 2020s, and I'm curious if that's just a matter of, well, at some point you sell enough. People know you, like you said, commanders, tell the commanders, captains, and word of mouth takes you there, or if something changed, either in a product or the market. That all of a sudden demand just kind of took a step change.
zh: 你现在是数千万级别了，对吧？在那个时候，你能指出某样东西吗？这个问题可能没有好的答案。反正我还是会问。是什么让你从更像是一种推销，嘿，我们在做数据，我们做得很好，一，三，十。这很棒，到像，哇，我们增长得这么快。我有这些其他问题？我问这个问题，你知道，只是为了我的客户。对我来说那就是，你知道，我们之前谈到的产品市场契合时刻。这实际上就像一个价值交付时刻，对吧？第一次这是一个行动，你解决了那个冷案，就像，好的，这东西行得通。这不一定等同于对此有如此多的需求。我淹没在需求中，这有点像你在 2020 年代谈论的那样，我很好奇这是否只是一个，嗯，在某个时刻你卖得足够多的问题。人们认识你，就像你说的，指挥官告诉指挥官，警长，口碑带你到达那里，或者有什么东西改变了，要么是在产品中，要么是在市场中。突然需求发生了阶跃变化。

speaker: Ben Rudolph
en: That demand, it's a mix of all of those and the moment that I really felt that we needed to teach it is, we were operating off of a spreadsheet for resourcing and how, who goes where. And, we just had this big list of customers and we had this small list of deployment folks. And they were all tied up in current customers. And we feel very strongly that like, as soon as the contract is signed, we got to start work on this. We got to start integrating data, we got to start providing the value and we were taking engineers off the line and doing core product work to be able to do these far deployed motions. And that is when we were really testing the scale of how we could develop that playbook to make it more efficient. How we could hire rapidly to be able to meet the demand.
zh: 那种需求，它是所有这些的混合体，我真正感觉到我们需要教授它的时刻是，我们是依靠电子表格来进行资源分配以及，谁去哪里的。而且，我们要有这个庞大的客户名单，我们只有这个简短的部署人员名单。而且他们都忙于当前的客户。我们非常强烈地感觉到，合同一签署，我们就得开始为此工作。我们得开始集成数据，我们得开始提供价值，而且我们正在让工程师脱离生产线去做核心产品工作，以便能够做这些远程部署动作。那就是当我们真正测试我们如何开发那个剧本以使其更高效的规模的时候。我们如何能够快速招聘以满足需求。

speaker: Pablo Srugo
en: And is that also when, just looking at your fundraise history. Would you say that that was also when fundraising really took off? Now you're raising massive rounds and I'm sure it's probably not hard for you to raise. I mean, you want to optimize and all these sort of things but I'm sure you've got more demand than supply in terms of fundraising.
